title: Breaking the barriers
hook: the manual's test: bandits demand one of four people; metta hands over none

segments.voice: Yesterday, the difficult person, met with a small, sincere wish. Your line was a little, honestly. Did the difficult person get one silent wish? Day one hundred and three.

Everybody's seen the lifeboat question. One seat left: who gets it? People argue about it at dinner parties and in philosophy classes. Fifteen hundred years ago, a Buddhist monk in Sri Lanka wrote his own version, as a test for anyone practicing metta. Four people are sitting together. Bandits burst in. They say: give us one of you. We're going to kill that one. Who do you hand over? It's a strange question for a book about kindness. But the answer is the point of the last six days.
screen: `THE LIFEBOAT QUESTION.` → `BANDITS BURST IN.` → `GIVE US ONE OF YOU.`

segments.voice: The monk is Buddhaghosa, and the test is in the ninth chapter of the Visuddhimagga. The four people are the ones you've practiced with this week. Yourself. A dear person. A neutral person. A hostile person. The bandits demand one. Now watch the manual's answers. If you think, take the enemy, your metta isn't finished: there's still a barrier around the one you dislike. If you think, take the stranger, the same. And here's the twist most people don't expect. If you think, take me, spare the others, that's not the answer either. It sounds noble. But the manual says it still shows a barrier, around yourself. You've made yourself the one who doesn't count. The test is passed only when you can't find anyone to hand over. Not the enemy, not the stranger, not the friend, not you. Each one's life weighs the same in your heart. That's what the manual calls breaking the barriers, sima-sambheda. The walls between the categories come down. Remember, this is a picture, not a plan for a real emergency. It's a way of checking where the walls still stand. Most of us, honestly, find a wall somewhere. And the manual doesn't shame anyone for that. It describes the goal: a mind where kindness no longer sorts people into loved, ignored and disliked. After six days of taking the categories one at a time, this is where they meet. Tomorrow, the circle opens all the way: every direction, every being.
screen: `FOUR PEOPLE, AND BANDITS.` · `TAKE THE ENEMY? A WALL.` · `TAKE ME? STILL A WALL.` · `NO ONE TO HAND OVER.` · then, large: `NO ONE HANDED OVER.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring four people to mind together, sitting in a row: yourself, someone dear, someone neutral, someone difficult. See all four. Now offer the phrases to all of them at once. May we be safe. May we be happy. May we be healthy. May we live with ease. Notice if the wish feels stronger for one and thinner for another. That's fine. That's the wall showing itself. Just keep the four together, and let the wish move evenly across the row. The bell holds the time.
Breaking the barriers. The manual's test of metta: when bandits demand one of four, you find no one to hand over.
Your line: no one handed over. Today, notice when you sort someone into a category, and remember all four in the row. Day one hundred and three.

howItsDone: Following the Visuddhimagga, Buddhist meditators aim to extend metta equally to themselves, dear, neutral and hostile persons, and teachers use the manual's bandit test to show what that evenness means.

fork.reveal: only when no one can be handed over, not even yourself, does the manual say the barriers are broken.

original.note: Pali: the breaking down of boundaries between persons in metta practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gruesome riddle.
what it means: a check on whether kindness still sorts people into loved, ignored and disliked.
what a scholar hears: Visuddhimagga IX presents the bandit test as the sign of sima-sambheda, after which the meditator develops the sign for absorption in metta.

notes: The bandit test is paraphrased from Visuddhimagga IX; confirm that the manual counts 'take me' as failing the test.
'Fifteen hundred years ago' assumes a fifth-century date for Buddhaghosa.
